title: Building Protected MCP Servers — Den Delimarsky and Julia Kasper, MCP Steering Committee & Microsoft

summary: The session addresses how to protect MCP servers, focusing on remote servers accessible over the internet. Den Delimarsky and Julia Kasper explain that many APIs MCP servers connect to require user context—different users have different permissions, admin policies, and tool access—so the MCP layer must expose identity. Local servers, by contrast, run as binaries on a machine and can use any credential type without constraint. The stable March 26 spec required developers building MCP servers to spin up their own authorization server, effectively becoming OAuth experts who mint, manage, refresh, and sign tokens themselves—very complicated and error-prone. The new draft spec, refined in partnership with Anthropic and security experts, cleanly separates the MCP server (now called the resource server) from the authorization server. Token minting and lifetime management are delegated to standard identity providers like Okta, Auth0, Microsoft Entra ID, or Keycloak. The flow works as follows: the MCP client requests data; the server responds with HTTP 401 and a pointer to a Protected Resource Metadata (PRM) document embedded in the WWW-Authenticate header; the client reads the PRM to discover the authorization server, supported bearer methods, and scopes; the client performs standard OAuth discovery and obtains a token; then it requests data with the token. A C# demo using ASP.NET Core and the official MCP C# SDK shows minimal configuration and end-to-end success: the client discovers metadata, obtains a token from Entra ID, the server validates it, and a weather tool is invoked. Julia then demonstrates production deployment using Azure API Management as a gateway proxy between clients and the remote MCP server, handling OAuth dance with Entra ID. An ARM template deploys resources in about five minutes including app service plan and log analytics. The MCP Inspector and VS Code both support the consent flow, and GitHub Copilot detects and runs the remote MCP tools. A new Azure API Management feature transforms existing REST APIs into remote MCP servers with OAuth security. Resources include spec documents, a security best practices document co-authored with Anthropic, and VS Code Insiders support for the new authorization spec.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Remote MCP servers need authorization because they connect to protected APIs requiring user context, while local servers face no such constraints as binaries on a machine.
The stable March 26 MCP spec required developers to build their own authorization server and become OAuth experts, minting and managing tokens themselves.
The new draft spec separates the MCP resource server from the authorization server, delegating token management to standard identity providers like Entra ID, Okta, Auth0, or Keycloak.
The Protected Resource Metadata (PRM) document is a JSON file hosted by the MCP server that tells clients which authorization server to use, supported bearer methods, and scopes.
In the new flow, the MCP client is responsible for the complete end-to-end OAuth token dance, while the server only validates tokens.
Azure API Management can serve as a production gateway proxy for remote MCP servers, handling OAuth authentication and consent flows with identity providers.
A new Azure API Management feature transforms existing REST API endpoints into remote MCP servers, making it easier for enterprise customers and developers to get started.
VS Code Insiders supports the new MCP authorization spec, allowing users to add remote MCP server endpoints and authenticate via OAuth consent flows.
Security best practices documentation co-authored with Anthropic is available to help developers avoid common pitfalls when building MCP servers.

sections.title: Introduction and Why Protected MCP Servers Matter
sections.summary: Den and Julia introduce themselves as Microsoft MCP squad members. They explain that remote MCP servers accessible over the internet need authorization because connected APIs require user context—different users have different permissions and admin policies. Local servers face no such constraints as binaries on a machine, where any credential type can be used. Multi-user VM scenarios are noted as out of scope.

sections.title: MCP Spec Evolution: From Token Factories to Separation of Concerns
sections.summary: Den explains two MCP spec versions: the stable March 26 spec, which required developers to build their own authorization server and mint tokens (requiring deep OAuth expertise), and a new draft spec developed with Anthropic and security experts. The draft cleanly separates the MCP resource server from the authorization server, letting standard identity providers handle token minting and lifetime management. Julia emphasizes this saves developers from writing risky security code.

sections.title: Authorization Flow and Protected Resource Metadata (PRM)
sections.summary: The presenters walk through the new authorization flow: client requests data, server returns 401 with a PRM pointer in the WWW-Authenticate header, client reads the PRM JSON document to discover authorization servers, bearer methods, and scopes, then completes the standard OAuth dance. The client handles the full token flow; the server only validates tokens.

sections.title: C# Demo: Protected MCP Server and Client Configuration
sections.summary: Den demonstrates a C# ASP.NET Core MCP server using the official MCP C# SDK (currently in a PR). Configuration involves adding MCP authentication defaults, PRM metadata pointing to Microsoft Entra ID, and standard framework token validation. The browser shows the PRM document. The client side uses a generic OAuth provider with a client ID and scopes, with no Microsoft-specific code.

sections.title: C# Client Demo Completion and Production with Azure API Management
sections.summary: The C# client successfully connects to the local server, discovers metadata, obtains a token from Entra ID, and the server validates it and invokes a weather tool. Julia then introduces Azure API Management as a production gateway proxy for remote MCP servers, using an ARM template (ACD app) to deploy resources in about five minutes, including app service plan and log analytics. The gateway handles OAuth authentication and consent flows with Microsoft Entra ID.

sections.title: Testing with MCP Inspector and VS Code Integration
sections.summary: Julia tests the remote MCP server through Azure API Management using MCP Inspector, showing the consent page and listing three tools. She then adds the endpoint in VS Code, completes the OAuth consent flow, and GitHub Copilot detects and runs the MCP tools successfully, returning output from a hello world example.

sections.title: REST API to MCP Server Transformation and Wrap-Up
sections.summary: Julia announces a new Azure API Management feature that transforms existing REST API endpoints into remote MCP servers with OAuth security, detected by GitHub Copilot in VS Code. Den wraps up by pointing to spec documents, a security best practices document co-authored with Anthropic, and notes that VS Code Insiders supports the new authorization spec, encouraging feedback and debugging help from Harold at the conference.

limitations: The draft authorization spec is not yet stable, though it is expected to become stable very soon.
Multi-user scenarios on VMs (e.g., remote desktop) are out of scope for MCP and left to implementers.
The C# SDK implementation shown is currently in a pull request, not yet merged into the official SDK.
Samples and tooling will continue to evolve as the MCP spec evolves.
